column4: The section contrasts the source wording أَنَّىٰ لَهُ الذِّكْرَىٰ, remembering after Hell is brought, with this open-time question to believers: has the time not come for hearts to humble at Allah’s remembrance? Here remembrance can still change the heart.

This asks أَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ الذِّكْرَىٰ after a clear messenger has come and they turned away; it directly parallels the section’s late “where/how can remembrance help?” and makes the prior opportunity part of the regret.

The source-section wording وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُ الذِّكْرَىٰ is echoed by فَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمْ إِذَا جَاءَتْهُمْ ذِكْرَاهُمْ: when the Hour comes, remembrance will not avail them. It confirms that the timing, not mere capacity to remember, closes the way.
The section’s cited memory scene at 79:35 begins when “the great calamity” comes; this neighbor supplies the arrival of that event as the threshold after which the human remembers.
This directly repeats the source section’s scene: on that day the human remembers ما سعى, what he strove for. It makes the belated memory specifically a review of one’s striving.
The section cites 79:35; this next ayah says Hell is exposed to whoever sees, completing the parallel sequence of calamity, remembrance, and displayed consequence.

The section cites وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ التَّنَاوُشُ مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ as an image of reaching from far away. This ayah’s own wording makes the missed object unreachable after the opportunity has passed, sharpening the distance in the section’s late-reaching hand.

The source section’s root ق د م and verb قَدَّمْتُ describe sending good ahead for “my life”; this command asks each soul to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow. It turns the later regret into a present practice.

This directly joins the section’s details: the person looks at what his two hands sent ahead, then the disbeliever says يَا لَيْتَنِي. Its own context makes the earlier deeds and the late wish one scene.
The section cites this day when a person is informed of what he sent ahead and left behind. It clarifies that the eventual review includes both deeds done and opportunities or traces left.
The section points to the day when a soul knows what it sent ahead and delayed. This concise parallel shows the late knowledge includes what was postponed, not only completed acts.

At death, a person asks for a short reprieve to give charity and become righteous; this is a concrete counterpart to the source section’s “if only I had sent ahead for my life,” showing the wish at the closing boundary of action.
The neighbor to 63:10 says Allah will not delay a soul when its appointed time comes. It supplies the answer that the section’s wish for more time cannot obtain.

This says repentance is accepted from those who do wrong in ignorance and then repent soon; beside the source section’s closed time of remembrance, it marks the earlier interval when turning back can still matter.
This explicitly excludes repentance only when death comes and one says “now I repent.” It gives the boundary between timely remembrance and the section’s too-late wish.
Before punishment arrives, this calls people to turn to their Lord and submit to Him. It states the open opportunity that the section’s later regret has lost.
The neighbor to 39:54 urges following the best revelation before punishment suddenly comes; this makes heedful action, rather than belated knowledge, the response available in time.
A soul says يَا حَسْرَتَىٰ over having neglected Allah’s side. It closely matches the section’s person who finally remembers and wishes he had prepared for his life.

The next excuse says that if Allah had guided the speaker, he would have been among the mindful. It parallels the section’s late realization while showing the speaker’s attempt to relocate responsibility.
On seeing punishment, a person wishes for another return so he can be among the doers of good. This is a direct parallel to the section’s regret over not sending good ahead.
The neighbor answers the excuses in 39:57–58 by recalling that Allah’s signs came and were denied with pride. It makes the missed reminder in the late wish concrete.
The section quotes 23:100’s refused return; this preceding ayah stages the trigger, death arriving and the person asking to be sent back. It places the wish at the moment life closes.
This directly supports the section’s claim that the dying person is told no when asking to return and do good. The barrier until resurrection explains why the life named in 89:24 cannot be restarted.
Seeing the Fire, people wish they could be returned and would not deny their Lord’s signs. This directly parallels memory and remorse after punishment has become visible.
The next ayah says that, if returned, they would go back to what was forbidden. It complicates the apparent sincerity of the late wish and cautions against treating regret as proof of changed action.
The guilty bow their heads before their Lord and ask to be returned so they can act righteously. It closely parallels the section’s last-minute wish for a life in which good was sent ahead.
The neighbor to 32:12 says guidance would have been given to every soul if Allah had willed, while the word concerning Hell is fulfilled. It completes the scene’s answer to the request for return.
This says to taste the punishment for forgetting the meeting of that day. The reversal of remembrance makes the section’s late recollection of the Hereafter especially pointed.

People in the Fire plead to be brought out to do good differently; the reply recalls that they were given a life span in which whoever would remember could remember. This is a direct account of the time the section says has closed.

The condemned admit their sins and ask for a way out after having died twice and been given life twice. It echoes the section’s recognition after judgment, though its focus is confession rather than preparation.
The neighbor explains that their rejection followed because when Allah alone was called they disbelieved. It grounds the preceding confession in the earlier refusal of the reminder.
When the true promise nears, disbelievers cry that they had been heedless of it and wronged themselves. This is another explicit awakening whose timing arrives with the event itself.

Those who took religion as play and were deluded by worldly life are told that day they will be forgotten as they forgot its meeting. This links the section’s late memory to an earlier turning away and preference.
The people who forgot meeting this day are told that they will now be forgotten and the Fire is their abode. It gives the same remembrance-forgetting reversal as the section’s late recognition.
This neighbor says their taking Allah’s signs in ridicule and being deluded by worldly life brought that outcome. It identifies the past that makes the preceding reversal apt.
The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger. This is a concrete late wish for a different course, like the section’s wish to have sent good ahead.
The neighbor continues the wish as regret over having taken a certain person as a friend. It adds the relationship that made the wrong path compelling.
The speaker says that the reminder came but he was led away from it. This completes the section’s specific link between late remembrance and an earlier reminder abandoned.
The section cites the person who says he wishes he had not received his book. The left-hand record makes the wish a response to an already disclosed account.
The next wish is that the speaker had not known his account. It completes the section’s book scene as regret over knowledge arriving with the judgment.
The same lament wishes that death had been final. It sharpens the section’s contrast between the life first misidentified and the afterlife that cannot be escaped.
The speaker admits his wealth has not availed him. This links the regret scene to the section’s account of mistaking provision and wealth for honor.
The speaker says his authority has perished. It completes the failed-wealth sequence beside the section’s judgment of what worldly status meant.
The record is laid open; wrongdoers fear its contents and find their deeds present. This directly parallels the section’s eventual look at what was sent ahead and the regret it provokes.
Each person’s record is fastened to him and brought out on Resurrection Day. This concretizes the section’s claim that the later reckoning concerns what each person himself prepared.
The person is told to read his book, with himself sufficient as reckoner. It makes the section’s belated self-recognition a direct encounter with one’s record.
Each soul finds the good and evil it did present, and wishes there were a great distance between itself and the evil. This is a specific parallel to seeing the past and wishing it were otherwise.
Whoever has done an atom’s weight of good will see it. It supplies a concrete scale for the deeds the section says one wishes had been sent ahead.
The paired ayah says whoever did an atom’s weight of evil will see it too. It completes the accounting with the opposite side of the deeds recalled.
There every soul is tested by what it sent forward, and they return to Allah, their true Lord. It joins the section’s qaddam root (sending ahead) to the return that makes life’s stakes visible.

The section’s source root ق د م names good deeds sent ahead; this command says whatever good is sent ahead for oneself will be found with Allah. It presents the future discovery as motivation before the section’s late scene.
This repeats that whatever good people send ahead for themselves they will find with Allah, greater in reward. It explicates the enduring result of the section’s earlier “sending ahead.”
The command to take provision for the journey, with taqwa named as the best provision, clarifies the section’s dictionary explanation of qaddama as good prepared and sent ahead to one’s destination.
The human is addressed as toiling toward his Lord and meeting Him. It makes explicit the journey-to-meeting that underlies the section’s “for my life” and the return to the Lord.
The person given his record in the right hand faces an easy reckoning, the opposite outcome to the late regret over a condemning account in the section’s cited 69:25.
The neighbor says that this person will be reckoned with an easy reckoning; it names the favorable judgment contrasting with the section’s belated realization.
The same person returns joyful to his family. It contrasts with the section’s person who recognizes too late that his life was not prepared well.
The other person receives his record from behind his back, an opposing record-delivery scene to the section’s cited left-hand book in 69:25.
The recipient of the record from behind calls for destruction. It adds a despairing response to the adverse judgment corresponding to the section’s “if only” lament.
The next ayah says he enters a blazing fire, completing the adverse record scene that contrasts with the section’s return of the tranquil soul to its Lord.

The section explicitly cites وَإِنَّ الدَّارَ الْآخِرَةَ لَهِيَ الْحَيَوَانُ: the Hereafter is the true life. It resolves the widening sense of the source section’s word “my life” and contrasts it with the life misread earlier.
The section’s life word ح ي ي meets a dying person who asks for a return to do good; the reply and barzakh make the ultimate life real while denying another worldly term.

Every soul tastes death, is paid in full on Resurrection Day, and the successful one is drawn away from Fire; worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment. This supports the section’s correction of what “my life” truly names.
People prefer the nearer life, directly reversing the section’s recognition that the Hereafter is the true life and that worldly preference leaves one with nothing sent ahead.
The paired ayah says the Hereafter is better and more enduring. It states the permanence that the section’s definition of life assigns to the afterlife.

This ayah identifies the one who transgresses, a specific moral outcome related to the section’s account of people misreading their trial; the next ayah identifies that transgressor’s preference for worldly life.
The next ayah says that the blazing fire is the refuge of the one who preferred worldly life, joining the section’s fire and corrected understanding of life.
This ayah names the Fire as the refuge in the scene that begins with the great calamity at 79:34; it completes the context of the section’s cited remembrance at 79:35.
The one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained the self from desire is set against the worldly preference in the section’s account of late regret.
The neighbor gives that restrained person the Garden as refuge, completing the contrast to the Fire and clarifying the life toward which the section’s soul is welcomed.

The command is to remind if the reminder benefits, and the following ayat divide those who fear and remember from those who avoid it. It closely matches the section’s open warning at 57:16 and late remembrance at 89:23.
The one who fears will remember. This directly connects remembrance with the stance the section’s warning seeks while time remains.
The most wretched avoids the reminder, a specific opposite to the fearful person who remembers in 87:10 and to the section’s addressed tranquil soul.
The one who avoids the reminder enters the great Fire, completing the contrast between present remembrance and the section’s post-Fire memory.
In the Fire he neither dies nor lives. This gives a specific boundary to the source section’s broad word “life” and contrasts with its claim that the Hereafter is true life.

Whoever turns away from Allah’s remembrance is promised a constricted life and is raised blind. This links forgetting remembrance to a life gone wrong and contrasts with the section’s life found only in the Hereafter.

The source section calls the final soul ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ; here believing hearts find rest (تَطْمَئِنُّ) in Allah’s remembrance. It gives a close Qur’anic parallel for the soul’s settled state and ties it to dhikr.

The source section explicitly labels the dictionary form التَّنَفُّس (breath leaving the inside) under root ن ف س; this oath describes dawn إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ, “when it breathes.” It is a lexical image parallel, though dawn’s breath is not a dying soul.

When the human is formed, Allah says He breathed into him from His spirit. This supplies the life-giving inward movement that balances the section’s image of breath going outward and souls being taken.

This repeats the breathing of Allah’s spirit into the human, followed by the angels’ prostration. It is another explicit creation scene illuminating the section’s dictionary sense of nafs as the spirit by which the body lives.

After forming the human, Allah breathes into him from His spirit and grants hearing, sight, and hearts. The life and faculties that follow clarify the section’s gloss of nafs as what gives the body life.

The section cites Allah’s taking of souls at death and in sleep. This ayah directly stages the distinction between the souls whose death is decreed and those released until a set term, giving the breath/soul movement concrete form.

Allah takes people at night, raises them by day, and returns them to it until their term is fulfilled. It parallels the section’s dictionary link between breath, soul, sleep, and bodily life, though it describes the cycle rather than a final soul’s welcome.

The section cites the angels’ command أَخْرِجُوا أَنفُسَكُمُ to wrongdoers at death and their humiliation. It supplies the forced extraction against which the tranquil soul’s invitation to return is contrasted.

After the death scene in 6:93, each person comes to God alone and has left behind what was given. This completes the section’s contrast between seized souls and the peaceful soul’s return, while showing worldly possessions do not accompany it.
At death the angels strike the faces and backs of those who disbelieved. This is a specific harsh extraction scene set against the section’s soul addressed gently and welcomed back.
The angels take the disbelievers’ souls while striking their faces and backs. It repeats the violent death scene that contrasts with the section’s unforced return of the tranquil soul.

Angels take the souls of those who wronged themselves; they offer submission at that moment, but their claim of having done no evil is rejected. This is a deathbed counterpart to the section’s contrast between the punished and the soul that returns content.
The angel of death is appointed over people and then they are returned to their Lord. This joins the section’s account of souls taken from bodies to its repeated destination, return to God.
The section cites the soul reaching the collarbones (التَّرَاقِيَ) at death. It sets that bodily crisis beside 89’s soul that is called and invited to return, clarifying the difference in manner.
The question “who can cure?” follows the soul reaching the collarbones in 75:26. It develops the deathbed scene that the section contrasts with the tranquil soul’s welcome.
The dying person recognizes that it is the parting, continuing the crisis in 75:26–27 before the section’s cited destination in 75:30.
The legs are brought together in the same death scene; it completes the bodily departure before 75:30 says the drive is to the Lord.
The section cites إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ: at death one is driven to the Lord. It contrasts this compelled passage with the content soul’s gentle imperative to return in 89:28.
This begins when the soul reaches the throat, directly echoing the section’s account of nafs as life-bearing and breath’s departure from within the body.
The people present look on as the soul reaches the throat; this continues the death scene that the section sets beside the calm soul’s welcome.
Allah is nearer to the dying person than the onlookers, though they do not perceive it. This adds the unseen divine presence to the section’s account of a soul’s final passage.
If the onlookers are not to be recompensed, they are challenged to bring the soul back. It directly stages the impossibility of reversing death that underlies the section’s denied wish for more life.
The challenge is repeated: bring the soul back if truthful. It makes the section’s contrast between the dead person’s helplessness and the addressed soul’s return especially concrete.
For a soul among those brought near, the death scene ends in comfort and provision. This is a specific favorable counterpart to the section’s tranquil soul.
The brought-near soul receives a Garden of bliss. It parallels the section’s return of the pleased soul to its Lord and entrance into His Garden.
The following branch concerns one of the companions of the right. It continues the deathbed outcomes around the welcomed soul of the section.
Peace is spoken to a companion of the right, completing the favorable death outcome and echoing the section’s welcome of the tranquil soul.

The steadfast are met by angels telling them not to fear or grieve and giving glad tidings of the Garden. It is a specific parallel to the soul in the section that is addressed and welcomed at its return.
The angels say they are allies in worldly life and the Hereafter. This continues the welcome in 41:30 and gives its assurance across both lives.
The angels describe the Garden as hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful One, completing the specific welcome that parallels the section’s final soul.
Angels receive the good at death saying peace and telling them to enter the Garden for what they did. This parallels the section’s content soul welcomed and admitted to the Garden.
The person admitted to the Garden is one who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a returning heart. It gives a concrete parallel to the section’s soul settled and returning to its Lord.
The next ayah says to enter the Garden in peace, the day of eternity. It completes the returning heart’s welcome in 50:33 and illuminates the section’s final admission.

The source section names the dictionary sense of ن ف س as soul; Yusuf says the soul strongly commands to evil except where his Lord has mercy. This is a morally unsettled state that contrasts with ٱلنَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ.
The source section’s soul-word is echoed by the self-reproaching soul (النَّفْسِ اللَّوَّامَةِ). Its self-reproach contrasts with the tranquil soul that has reached rest.
The oath names the soul and the One who fashioned it. This supports the section’s treatment of nafs as a living inner self, though it does not itself describe the death or return scene.
The soul is shown its wickedness and piety. This gives content to the inner condition whose final settled form the section describes.
The soul that is purified succeeds. This is a concrete moral counterpart to the tranquil soul’s favorable return, in contrast with the condemned soul’s belated regret.
The soul that is corrupted fails, a direct contrary outcome to the settled and welcomed soul in the section.

On the Day when wealth and children do not benefit, worldly goods cannot secure the outcome the regretful person wants. This directly answers the section’s account of wealth being mistaken for honor and later regret.
Only one who comes to Allah with a sound heart is excepted from that loss. This offers a specific heart-state parallel to the section’s tranquil soul returning pleased and pleasing.
Every soul tastes death; people are tested with good and evil and returned to Allah. This brings together the section’s soul, its note that life’s trial is misread, and the return after the test.
Death and life are created to test who is best in deeds. This gives an explicit frame for the section’s correction of the opening claims that comfort means honor and constraint means humiliation.
This ayah says the human transgresses, directly illuminating the section’s earlier account of misreading abundance as honor before later regret.
The next ayah says the human sees himself self-sufficient, completing the specific cause of transgression that the section says the first two utterances misread.
The human’s return is to his Lord. This completes the self-sufficiency scene with the return that exposes the mistake described in the section.
